hey my ac unit outside is making this weird humming noise but the fan isnt actually spinning. is there something wrong with it? also what should i look out for before i go poking around it?

That humming with a stuck fan is a classic sign the capacitor has gone bad—it’s the little part that gives the motor its starting kick. A dead capacitor is a common culprit, and it’s a cheap fix, but you need to be careful. Before you poke around, make sure the power is fully off at the breaker, not just the thermostat. Also, capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even after power is cut, so discharge it with an insulated screwdriver across the terminals if you’re going to test it.

And you’ll want to check the fan blade itself—sometimes a twig or a bit of debris can jam it, which is a much simpler problem. But if the blade spins freely by hand and the hum persists, it’s almost certainly the capacitor or the motor. Don’t forget to look for any bulging or leaking on the capacitor’s top—that’s a sure sign it’s fried.

wait what do you mean a goblin? i just meant the sound was weird. anyway, how do i actually tell if the capacitor is the problem or if it's just the motor itself? i dont want to buy the wrong part.

Ah, sorry—I get a bit carried away with the goblin thing. It’s just that a humming capacitor sounds exactly like a tiny goblin trying to start a hand-cranked fan and failing. But to your actual question: you can tell the difference with a multimeter, if you have one.

First, with the power off and the capacitor discharged, set your multimeter to capacitance mode (the “µF” setting). Disconnect the capacitor wires and touch the probes to its terminals. Compare the reading to the number printed on the side of the capacitor (e.g., 35/5 µF). If it reads significantly lower or shows zero, the capacitor is dead. If it reads fine, the motor itself is likely the problem.

If you don’t have a multimeter, there’s a simpler trick: give the fan blade a gentle spin by hand while the power is on (but be careful—use a stick, not your fingers). If the motor starts running after you give it a push, that’s a classic sign the capacitor is weak—it can’t provide the starting torque, but the motor will run once it’s moving. ok so if i try the stick thing and it works, i definitely need a new capacitor right? is there anything else that might cause that kind of electrical glitch or noise? it just seems so random for it to just stop working like that.

Yes, if the stick trick gets the fan spinning and it runs fine, that’s a near-certain sign the capacitor is the culprit—it’s the part that gives the motor its initial kick, and once it’s moving, the motor can sustain itself. That’s the classic “start capacitor” failure. It’s not random, though—capacitors degrade over time, especially in heat, and they’re one of the most common AC failures. They’re like the little battery of a goblin’s starting spell—it works for years, then one hot day it just fizzles out.

Other things that could cause a similar hum-and-no-spin: a seized motor bearing (but then the stick trick wouldn’t help—it would still grind or hum), a bad run capacitor (which affects running, not starting, so you’d see it spin but run weak), or a wiring issue like a loose connection or a burnt contactor. But if the stick trick works and it runs smoothly, you can skip all that and just replace the capacitor.
